finding.claim: The current user is taken directly from a client-supplied HTTP header (X-Session-User-Verified) with no session, signature or proxy validation. Any caller can impersonate any user by setting this header to a username listed in a resource's grants. This bypasses all ACL checks for delete and rename.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled request header X-Session-User-Verified, sent by any unauthenticated remote client
finding.sink: del STORE[fid] in delete_file (views.py:18) and f["name"] assignment in rename_file (views.py:27)

trace.note: g.user is set from the raw header value, with no authentication
is_allowed only checks whether the claimed username appears in resource grants, so a spoofed name passes
the same trust applies to the write check in rename_file

finding.guards_checked: Searched the whole repo (only acl.py and views.py exist). There is no auth middleware, no signature or HMAC check, and no stripping of the header at a trusted proxy. The name suggests an upstream proxy sets it, but nothing in the code enforces that, and a direct request can set it. If a trusted gateway strips and re-sets the header, the severity drops. The ACL logic in acl.py itself is sound: a missing user yields None, which has no grants.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (aborts 403) and is_allowed (checked, returns 403) in acl.py:4-10 are correctly used, but they only check the claimed username against grants. No authentication, signature check or proxy-header stripping exists in the repo.
verdict.reason: views.py:11 sets g.user from the raw X-Session-User-Verified header and the ACL checks at views.py:17 and views.py:25 (acl.py:5) trust it, so any client who knows or guesses a granted username can delete or rename; the only open question is whether an unseen gateway strips the header.
